payload.rationale: Observed: CDC reports 3,471 confirmed 2026 US cases as of Sept 17, 2026 (39 outbreaks, 95% outbreak-associated), versus 2,289 for all of 2025. Reaching >6,000 requires roughly 2,530 additional cases with onset in the remaining ~15 weeks of the year, i.e. about 170/week sustained. The year-to-date average is ~94/week, and that average almost certainly includes a large late-winter/spring peak, so the current run-rate is likely well below the average. Measles transmission in the US is seasonally weaker in autumn/early winter, and even the largest recent US outbreak (West Texas 2025, ~760 cases) accumulated over many months. Nearly doubling the annual-average weekly incidence during the off-peak season, plus reporting lag (cases assigned by rash-onset week and late-December cases may not be counted before expiration, with post-expiration revisions excluded), makes YES unlikely. Too-low risk: I lack the recent weekly series; if several large outbreaks in undervaccinated communities are currently accelerating (39 outbreaks is a lot) and school-term transmission compounds, 150–200+/week is not impossible, as late-2025 South Carolina growth showed fall outbreaks can be substantial. Too-high risk: if current weekly counts are in the tens, even 4,500 would be a stretch and the true probability is closer to 1–2%. Transfer assumptions: seasonality patterns from prior years and no major new importation-driven surge. Estimate ~5%.
limitations: No weekly incidence series or trend data supplied; current transmission rate is inferred, not observed.
CDC counts are provisional; reporting lag and year-assignment by rash onset affect the final pre-expiration figure.
Single-source packet; no fitted epidemic model.
